QF.id: AIFM CIII AIFs in India and Suitability_11

question.text: Mr. Deepak Sharma (age 44) has a INR 100 crore portfolio: 25% large-cap equities, 25% small-cap equities, 20% unlisted equity, 15% listed corporate debt, 10% G-Secs, 5% money market. His asset-class concentration cap is 40%. He wants to re-deploy the unlisted equity sleeve into ONE of two Cat III AIFs: Fund P (long-short, mid-cap only, 3-yr horizon) or Fund Q (market-neutral, 80% small-cap + 20% mid-cap). Which is the appropriate choice and why?

answer.text: Fund Q, because market-neutral funds always dominate long-short on risk-adjusted terms
Split 50:50 between Fund P and Fund Q to maximise manager diversification
Fund P, because reallocating to Fund Q would push direct+indirect small-cap exposure above the 40% concentration cap
Neither — Cat III AIFs are unsuitable for an investor with an existing unlisted equity allocation

explanation.text: The Logic: Adapting Example 4.1: small-cap is already 25% of the portfolio. Fund Q (80% small-cap of a 20% sleeve = 16% additional small-cap) would push small-cap exposure to 25% + 16% = 41%, breaching the 40% asset-class cap. Fund P (mid-cap only) avoids the breach. The chapter's solution is to allocate the INR 20 crore to Fund P. The Trap: Option A makes a blanket risk-adjusted claim not supported by facts. Option B ignores the concentration breach. Option D misreads suitability — Cat III is appropriate for this UHNI profile. Cross-Exam Context: This Example-4.1 pattern recurs in XIX-B and XIX-C. XIX-E frames it from the Manager's angle — you are underwriting the subscription and documenting suitability, not just advising.
